Exercises

Problems to check your understanding of this chapter. The solutions are folded away — try them yourself first.

Easy

1Easy

A consumer reports (5,1)≻(3,3)(5, 1) \succ (3, 3)(5,1)≻(3,3) and (3,3)≻(2,4)(3, 3) \succ (2, 4)(3,3)≻(2,4). If the preference relation ≿\succsim≿ is complete and transitive, what can be said about (5,1)(5, 1)(5,1) versus (2,4)(2, 4)(2,4)?

x≻y  ⟺  x≿y and not y≿xx \succ y \iff x \succsim y \text{ and not } y \succsim xx≻y⟺x≿y and not y≿x
  • Preference Relations and Axioms
Show solution
  1. Strict preference ≻\succ≻ is transitive whenever ≿\succsim≿ is complete and transitive. From (5,1)≻(3,3)(5,1) \succ (3,3)(5,1)≻(3,3) and (3,3)≻(2,4)(3,3) \succ (2,4)(3,3)≻(2,4) we get (5,1)≻(2,4)(5, 1) \succ (2, 4)(5,1)≻(2,4).
  2. Proof sketch of transitivity: let x≿yx \succsim yx≿y, ¬(y≿x)\lnot(y \succsim x)¬(y≿x), y≿zy \succsim zy≿z, ¬(z≿y)\lnot(z \succsim y)¬(z≿y). Transitivity gives x≿zx \succsim zx≿z. If z≿xz \succsim xz≿x held, then y≿z≿xy \succsim z \succsim xy≿z≿x would give y≿xy \succsim xy≿x, a contradiction. Hence ¬(z≿x)\lnot(z \succsim x)¬(z≿x), i.e. x≻zx \succ zx≻z.

3Medium

The consumer chose x=(20,40)x = (20, 40)x=(20,40) at (p,w)=((1,1),60)(p, w) = ((1, 1), 60)(p,w)=((1,1),60) and y=(25,25)y = (25, 25)y=(25,25) at (p′,w′)=((3,1),100)(p', w') = ((3, 1), 100)(p′,w′)=((3,1),100). Compute the revealed-preference relations and decide whether WARP is violated.

p⋅x=60,p′⋅y=100p \cdot x = 60, \quad p' \cdot y = 100p⋅x=60,p′⋅y=100
  • Choice Rules and WARP
Show solution
  1. Budget check: p⋅x=20+40=60≤60p \cdot x = 20 + 40 = 60 \le 60p⋅x=20+40=60≤60 and p′⋅y=75+25=100≤100p' \cdot y = 75 + 25 = 100 \le 100p′⋅y=75+25=100≤100 — both bundles are affordable.
  2. In situation 1, yyy costs p⋅y=25+25=50≤60=p⋅xp \cdot y = 25 + 25 = 50 \le 60 = p \cdot xp⋅y=25+25=50≤60=p⋅x. Since yyy was affordable, x≿∗yx \succsim^* yx≿∗y.
  3. In situation 2, xxx costs p′⋅x=60+40=100≤100=p′⋅yp' \cdot x = 60 + 40 = 100 \le 100 = p' \cdot yp′⋅x=60+40=100≤100=p′⋅y. Since xxx was affordable, y≿∗xy \succsim^* xy≿∗x. Revealed preference holds both ways between two distinct bundles, so WARP is violated.

Hard

4Hard

Pairwise choices over the three bundles A=(4,4)A = (4, 4)A=(4,4), B=(5,2)B = (5, 2)B=(5,2), C=(2,5)C = (2, 5)C=(2,5) came out as follows (each pair has a unique winner): AAA beats BBB, BBB beats CCC, and CCC beats AAA. Prove that no complete and transitive preference relation ≿\succsim≿ rationalizes all three choices.

A chosen over B,B chosen over C,C chosen over AA \text{ chosen over } B, \quad B \text{ chosen over } C, \quad C \text{ chosen over } AA chosen over B,B chosen over C,C chosen over A
  • Preference Relations and Axioms
  • Choice Rules and WARP
Show solution
  1. Suppose ≿\succsim≿ rationalizes the three choices. That AAA alone was chosen from {A,B}\{A, B\}{A,B} means A≿BA \succsim BA≿B and ¬(B≿A)\lnot(B \succsim A)¬(B≿A), i.e. A≻BA \succ BA≻B. Likewise B≻CB \succ CB≻C and C≻AC \succ AC≻A.
  2. Since ≿\succsim≿ is complete and transitive, so is ≻\succ≻ (the proof in exercise 1). From A≻BA \succ BA≻B and B≻CB \succ CB≻C we get A≻CA \succ CA≻C.
  3. But C≻AC \succ AC≻A means C≿AC \succsim AC≿A and ¬(A≿C)\lnot(A \succsim C)¬(A≿C), while A≻CA \succ CA≻C requires A≿CA \succsim CA≿C — a contradiction. Hence no such ≿\succsim≿ exists. This is what breaks when transitivity fails: cycling choices are explained by no rational preference, and in revealed-preference terms they are a WARP violation A≿∗B≿∗C≿∗AA \succsim^* B \succsim^* C \succsim^* AA≿∗B≿∗C≿∗A.
